title: Don't Memorize Trigonometric Identities. Visualize Them Instead.
author: What Schools Forget
summary: A math educator recounts freezing on a quantum mechanics final exam because a trigonometric identity, memorized eight years earlier in high school, had simply evaporated — and uses that personal failure to argue for teaching mathematical identities as derivable pictures rather than memorized formulas. The core distinction driving the piece is that memorization and understanding fail differently: when a memorized fact is gone, it's gone completely, but a derivable understanding leaves 'the road back to it' even after the specific result is forgotten. Working through the angle-sum identities with diagrams of stacked right triangles inscribed in a circle, the author shows how sin(α+β) and cos(α+β) can be derived geometrically from similar triangles rather than looked up, tracing the method back to Ptolemy's second-century derivation using inscribed quadrilaterals. The practical recommendation is a direct pedagogical prescription: don't hand students the angle-sum formulas at all — give them the picture and have them derive the identity themselves, so that even if they forget the specific result, they retain the method to reconstruct it. A closing quotation from Descartes' La Géométrie reinforces the argument that withholding a derivation, rather than supplying it, is itself the pedagogical gift, since the effort of deriving something is 'the principal benefit to be derived from this science.'
points: The essay's key mechanism — 'when memorization fails, it fails completely. Understanding fails differently. You lose the result and keep the road back to it' — gives a memorable, generalizable justification for derivation-based teaching that extends well beyond trigonometry.

By tracing the geometric derivation of the angle-sum identities back to Ptolemy's second-century use of inscribed quadrilaterals, the piece grounds a modern pedagogical recommendation in a genuinely ancient mathematical method, reinforcing that visual derivation isn't a novel gimmick.

The explicit teaching prescription — 'Don't give the angle sum identities to students. Give them the picture... and get them to derive the identity for themselves' — is a concrete, actionable classroom instruction rather than an abstract call for 'more conceptual understanding.'
quotes: I had memorized the angle sum identities in high school using patterns. But I had no clear conception of why the identities were true.

We often teach mathematical formulas as things to learn by memorization. But when memorization fails, it fails completely. Understanding fails differently. You lose the result and keep the road back to it.
Using inscribed quadrilaterals, Ptolemy derived the chord version of these same identities in the second century.
On that quantum mechanics final, my memorized table of trig identities didn't work. What I needed was a simple picture: a circle and two stacked triangles. A few marks in a margin.

Don't give the angle sum identities to students. Give them the picture of right triangles stacked in a circle, ask them to draw sin(α + β), and get them to derive the identity for themselves. They will remember it, and if they forget it, they will be able to get it back.

I shall not stop to explain this in more detail, because I should deprive you of the pleasure of mastering it yourself, as well as of the advantage of training your mind by working over it, which is in my opinion the principal benefit to be derived from this science.
